name: A model that flags risky pull requests is tested on ten PRs that were not used in learning. It calls 4 of them risky, and 3 of those really had a bug; in total 5 of the ten PRs had a bug. Compute its accuracy, precision and recall (give the formulas) and name the two kinds of error. Under which three conditions does the score on a test set say how the model will do on new data?
answer:
Counts. True positives (called risky, had a bug): \(TP = 3\). False alarms: \(FP = 4 - 3 = 1\). Missed bugs: \(FN = 5 - 3 = 2\). True negatives: \(TN = 10 - 3 - 1 - 2 = 4\).
Metrics. \[\text{accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{\text{all}} = \frac{3 + 4}{10} = 70\,\%\] – the average of the verdicts, with right = 1 and wrong = 0. \[\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{3}{4} = 75\,\%,\qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{3}{5} = 60\,\%\] Precision says how often an alarm is real; recall says how many of the real bugs are found. The errors are of two kinds: one false alarm and two missed bugs.
Conditions. The average predicts behaviour on new data only if (1) the test set is kept apart from learning – being right on a row the weights were fitted to shows nothing; (2) the known outcomes are right; (3) the test set is like the data we care about – usually one collection is split at random, so the test set resembles the training set; for pull requests of another project the 70 % may not hold.
keyPoints: Accuracy \(= (TP + TN)/\text{all} = 7/10 = 70\,\%\)
Precision \(= TP/(TP + FP) = 3/4\); recall \(= TP/(TP + FN) = 3/5\)
Two kinds of error: false alarms and missed bugs
Conditions: test set kept apart, outcomes correct, test set like the target data

name: What is a classical ML benchmark, and why is building one hard? Illustrate with a large image-classification benchmark such as ImageNet.
answer: A benchmark is a published data set with labels, already split into a training and a test set; everybody trains on the same training set and reports the score on the same test set, so models from different teams can be compared on a leaderboard. The conditions for a meaningful score become assumptions about one shared test set: it played no role in building the model, its labels are correct, and it looks like the data you care about. Why it is hard (ImageNet challenge: 1,000 classes, over a million training images): candidate images came from image search engines queried in several languages; crowd workers (Amazon Mechanical Turk) marked which images showed the class; because single workers make mistakes and do not always follow instructions, several workers judged each image and it was kept only with a convincing majority. The test labels were kept secret, and a hand check still found a few wrong ones. The task is hard for people too: researchers labelling test images made many mistakes and improved a lot only after first training on hundreds of labelled examples. Because this is so much work, a test set is built once and reused for about a decade – which leads to the later problems of reuse, label errors and saturation.
keyPoints: Shared, published train/test split; a leaderboard compares teams
Assumptions: test set unseen, correctly labelled, representative
Labelling at scale: search-engine candidates, crowd workers, majority votes
Even careful labelling leaves errors; the task is hard for people too
Expensive → built once and reused for years

name: Researchers repeated the original data collection of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet to get new test images, and re-tested models that had been developed on the old test sets. What hypothesis did this test, what was expected, what was found, and what is the lesson?
answer: For years every paper reported on the same test set, and a model was kept if it scored better on it – so adaptive overfitting to the test set was suspected: is the progress real, or only progress on these test images? Recht et al. (2018–19) repeated the original collection to get new test images (a few thousand for CIFAR-10, 10,000 for ImageNet, from similar years, labelled by crowd workers as originally) and tested the old models. Expected: if the models had overfitted to the old test set, the newest, most tuned models should lose the most. Found: every model dropped (e.g. about 11–14 points on ImageNet; ResNet-152 from about 78 % to 67 %), but all by a similar amount, and “the relative order of models is almost exactly preserved”. The authors conclude that the drops come not from adaptivity but from the models’ inability to generalise to slightly “harder” images than those in the original test sets. Lesson: a benchmark score is a property of the model and of one particular test set; the preserved ranking held for these image classifiers and is not a general rule.
keyPoints: Hypothesis: adaptive overfitting to a reused test set
New test images collected the same way; old models re-tested
All models dropped by a similar amount; ranking almost exactly preserved
Cause: not adaptivity but weaker generalisation to slightly harder images
A score belongs to model + test set; stable rankings are not guaranteed elsewhere

name: How common are label errors in widely used test sets, how were they measured, and why do they matter?
answer: Northcutt et al. (NeurIPS 2021) searched ten widely used test sets. A trained classifier predicted a class for every test item, and items where it was confident of a different class than the given label were flagged; five Mechanical Turk workers then saw each flagged item, and it counted as an error if fewer than three agreed with the given label. Only flagged items were checked, so the numbers are lower bounds. Even MNIST – ten classes of clean digits, used for over 20 years – has wrong test labels (about 0.15 %); CIFAR-100 and the ImageNet validation set have several percent (about 6 %), a large drawing data set about 10 %. Why it matters: a model that is right gets marked wrong and a model that learned the mistake gets marked right; rankings can change (e.g. on ImageNet with corrected labels, ResNet-18 outperforms ResNet-50 if the share of originally mislabelled test examples rises by just 6 %); and two models that differ by less than the label error rate cannot be reliably told apart by the benchmark.
keyPoints: A classifier flags confident disagreements; crowd workers confirm errors
The counts are lower bounds (only flagged items were checked)
Even the cleanest, most used test sets have wrong labels; large ones several percent
Right models are penalised and mistaken ones rewarded; rankings can flip
Differences smaller than the label error rate are not meaningful

name: Explain benchmark saturation and Goodhart’s law. Illustrate with at least one example of each.
answer: Saturation: a benchmark gets “solved” and stops separating models. On the ImageNet challenge the winner’s error fell from about 28 % (2010) to about 2 % (2017), passing a trained person’s roughly 5 % in 2015. MNIST took over a decade to reach near-human performance, ImageNet about five years, and newer data sets now reach that milestone within a few years. Solving the benchmark does not mean the task is solved. Goodhart’s law (usually quoted as “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”; originally about monetary policy) says that a score tells you something about ability only as long as nobody works on the score itself; once models are selected, tuned and advertised by it, it says less. Examples: models chosen by their score on one reused test set; a team in 2015 made about 200 submissions in half a year to the ImageNet test server (allowed: two per week) and was asked to stay away for a year; gains of tenths of a point reported on benchmarks that no longer separate models.
keyPoints: Saturation: the winners’ error falls below human level and the benchmark stops separating models
The time to human level keeps shrinking
Solved benchmark ≠ solved task
Goodhart: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
Examples: selection on one reused test set, excessive test-server submissions, gains of tenths of a point

name: Describe how the MMLU and SWE-bench benchmarks work in terms of input, output, reference, grader and score.
answer: MMLU (2020) is an exam with four options per question: thousands of test questions from dozens of subjects, collected by students from practice exams online. Input: a question with four options; output: text from which a letter A–D is read; reference: the letter of the right option; grader: are the letters equal; score: share of right answers (guessing gives 25 %). SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024) uses real GitHub issues: from pull requests in a dozen popular Python repositories, scripts kept merged PRs that close an issue and change tests, and tasks that install and run with a test failing before and passing after the fix. Input: the issue and the repository before the fix; output: a patch, usually written by an agent with tools; reference: the tests from the real fix – FAIL_TO_PASS (fail before, must pass) and PASS_TO_PASS (must keep passing); only the test files changed by the fix are run; grader: apply the patch and run the tests, resolved if all pass; score: share of tasks resolved (at release the best model solved only a tiny share). The model sees neither the tests nor the fix. Variants: a smaller Lite subset and Verified (human-filtered tasks).
keyPoints: MMLU: 4-option questions, letter compared to key, share correct
SWE-bench: issue + repo in, patch out
Reference = hidden tests: FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS
Resolved = all those tests pass; only changed test files run
Tasks collected automatically by scripts; Lite and Verified are smaller subsets

name: How can a benchmark’s input be compromised for LLMs? Discuss contamination (the model has seen the items) and solutions present in the input, with evidence from MMLU and SWE-bench. How can contamination be detected or reduced?
answer: Why: LLMs are trained on web text, and benchmarks are public together with their references. MMLU: one test hides a wrong option of a question and asks the model to fill it in. Strong chat models reproduced the hidden option word for word in about half of the cases – knowing wrong options exactly is strong evidence that the model has read the test. SWE-bench: the same agent and model solved far fewer new issues (created since 2024, from 93 repositories) than Verified tasks – roughly 19 % instead of 43 % – with the caveat that the new issues are also different and unfiltered. Given only the issue text and the repository name, without any code, models named the file to fix in most Verified tasks, less often for other repositories: part of a Verified score is memory of twelve well-known code bases, and nobody knows how large a part. Solution in the input: some tasks contain the fix in the issue itself (e.g. an issue that proposes the exact method to add, so solving means copying three lines); one preprint found this in about a third of the tasks an early agent solved – a hint, not a firm rate. What the items stand for: MNIST measures exactly its task, but LLM benchmarks carry names much wider than their items: “75 % of SWE-bench Verified” means resolving about 375 mostly small issues in twelve Python libraries. Detection and countermeasures: fill-in probes for memorised items; testing on items created after the model was trained (live sets of new issues); keeping test items or labels private (ImageNet’s test labels, most SWE-bench Pro tasks); and, for your own decisions, measuring on tasks from your own repository.
keyPoints: Public benchmarks + training on the web → contamination
Models recite hidden wrong options → they have read the test
The same agent solves far fewer new issues than well-known ones; files to fix guessed without code
Some tasks give the solution in the issue
Benchmark names are wider than what their items measure
Countermeasures: new items, private test sets, fill-in probes, your own tasks
source: Lecture 4, slides 7, 21–24, 36, 49 (countermeasures synthesised from these slides)

name: Show that a benchmark score depends not only on the model but also on how the test is run. Give one example for the prompt format and one for the harness or the evaluation environment.
answer: Prompt format (MMLU): a study changed only how the same questions were asked of 11 open models – the order of the options (shuffled, or the right answer always in one position), their symbols (e.g. $ & # @ instead of A B C D) and how the model’s choice is read (most probable letter vs most probable answer text). Models moved by several places in the ranking (up to 8 of 11; shuffling alone up to 5). One reason: models prefer certain option letters. So a ranking can depend on the way of asking, not only on the model. Harness (SWE-bench Verified): the same model on the same 500 tasks solved between about 65 % and 70 % depending on the harness (bash-only, SWE-agent, OpenHands). A leaderboard entry is a model in a harness; entries with different harnesses do not compare models. Environment: an agent ran git log --all inside the evaluation container, which still held the commits made after the issue, and could find the actual fix (the later history was then removed). And the grader read printed test output, so a patch printing “PASSED <test name>” could count as solved – it is not known that a ranked model did this; the grader now also checks the exit code, though a way around that has already been reported. The agent is rewarded for “the tests pass”; solving the issue must be the only way to get there.
keyPoints: Prompt format: option order, symbols and how the choice is read change the ranking
Models prefer certain option letters
Harness: the same model scores several points apart in different harnesses
Environment loopholes: future git history readable; grader fooled by printed PASSED
Compare models in one harness and setup; solving the task must be the only way to pass

name: What can go wrong with the reference (answer key or tests) of a benchmark? Discuss errors in the MMLU answer key, and tests that are too strict and too weak in SWE-bench.
answer: MMLU: people re-checked a sample of questions (100 per subject) and estimated that a few percent of all questions contain an error, with some subjects far worse – unclear questions or options, no correct option, several correct options, or a wrong key (e.g. \(-47 = g + 24\) keyed as −23, although \(g = -71\)). On the corrected questions the model ranking changes. Cause: the key was copied from websites and never verified item by item. Too strict tests (SWE-bench): an issue only asks whether an unused copy parameter of a scikit-learn vectorizer is a mistake, but the hidden test requires a DeprecationWarning with an exact message decided later by the maintainers – other reasonable fixes (making the parameter work, removing it, warning in other words) fail. When SWE-bench Verified was built, developers reviewed a large sample of tasks (three reviewers per task): over a third had underspecified issues and well over half had tests that may reject a valid solution; about two thirds of the tasks were removed (one objection was enough). “Verified” means filtered, not rewritten. Too weak tests: for a seaborn issue about a value missing only in x, the hidden test only covers rows where both x and y are missing, so a patch that ignores missing x still passes. Adding tests to a few Lite tasks showed that over a quarter of the previously passing patches were wrong, and the ranks of many agents changed; running all repository tests instead of only the changed test files made several percent of “solved” patches fail. The Verified reviewers looked only for too strict tests, not for too weak ones.
keyPoints: MMLU: a few percent of items are wrong; the key was never verified
Too strict: a hidden test demands one exact solution the issue does not describe
Verified: about two thirds of tasks removed by reviewers; filtered, not fixed
Too weak: tests miss the issue’s case, so wrong patches pass
Better references change rankings

name: In a blind review study, maintainers of real open-source projects reviewed agent patches that pass the SWE-bench tests, mixed with the original human patches as a control. Describe the design, what they found, and what “resolved” therefore means.
answer: METR, an independent evaluation lab, gave about 300 agent patches that pass the SWE-bench tests (from published runs, models of mid-2024 to late 2025, one attempt per task) and 47 original human patches (all merged in reality, as a control) to four active maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest, who reviewed them as pull requests without being told who wrote them. They would merge about 68 % of the human patches – so a review is not an exact grader either – but only about a third of the agent patches (roughly half the human rate). Reasons for rejection: the patch does not really solve the issue or breaks other code and the tests did not catch it, or the code is poor in style and ignores project conventions, which tests do not check. A stated limit: the agent had one attempt and no feedback, whereas a human usually gets review feedback and tries again. Conclusion: “resolved” means these tests pass, not that a maintainer would take it. (This also shortens METR’s time horizon: for Claude Sonnet 4.5 about 50 minutes with test verdicts vs about 8 minutes with maintainer verdicts.)
keyPoints: Blind review of test-passing agent patches, with human patches as a control
Not all human patches were accepted → a review is not an exact grader either
Agent patches were accepted at roughly half the human rate
Rejections: not really fixed, breaks other code, poor style or conventions
Limit: one attempt, no review feedback
Tests passing ≠ mergeable

name: Why can two reported benchmark scores often not be compared directly? Discuss task subsets, cost, run-to-run variance, multiple attempts (pass@k, pass^k) and confidence ranges. Include two computations: (a) a vendor reports 74.9 % on 477 of a benchmark’s 500 tasks – what range does this imply for all 500 tasks? (b) a model solves 75 % of 500 tasks – roughly how wide is its 95 % range, and can it be ranked above a model with 77 %?
answer:
Task subsets. (a) \(0.749 \cdot 477 \approx 357\) tasks solved. On all 500 tasks the score lies between \(357/500 = 71.4\,\%\) (all 23 missing tasks fail) and \((357 + 23)/500 = 76.0\,\%\) (all of them solved). So a 477-task number cannot be put next to a 500-task number. (This was GPT-5’s announced SWE-bench Verified score; the note under it said so.)
Cost. Five models in one harness on the same 50 tasks cost from a few dollars to over a thousand – a factor of almost 300; the most expensive run was not the best, and the same score was reached by another model at about a third of the cost. A score does not say what was spent.
Run-to-run variance. Output is sampled, so each run is one draw of many possible scores; ten runs of the same setting differed by about 2–6 points, even at temperature 0, because the computation itself is not exactly repeatable.
Attempts. One model on 500 tasks: pass@1 (a single attempt) about 64 %, pass@5 (at least one of five attempts passes) about 76 %, pass^5 (all five pass) about 49 %. pass@k is a best case that needs someone to know which attempt is right – in your project nobody does; pass^k measures reliability.
Confidence range. (b) Treating the 500 tasks as a sample of all such tasks, the 95 % range is about \[\pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.75 \cdot 0.25}{500}} \approx \pm 0.038,\] i.e. 75 % ± 3.8 points (71.2–78.8 %). The other model’s 77 % lies inside this range, so from the two numbers alone the models cannot be ranked (with per-task results one could compare task by task). Few benchmark papers report any uncertainty (about one in six).
keyPoints: Subset: \(357/500 = 71.4\,\%\) to \(380/500 = 76.0\,\%\) – not comparable with a 500-task score
Cost can differ by orders of magnitude for similar scores; the most expensive run is not the best
Repeated runs differ by several points, even at temperature 0
pass@k is a best case needing an oracle; pass^k measures reliability
95 % range on 500 tasks \(\approx \pm 3.8\) points, so 75 % vs 77 % is a tie
Uncertainty is rarely reported
source: Lecture 4, slides 37–42 (the range formula is general statistics; the slide gives only the result)

name: What is METR’s time horizon of a model, how is it measured, what trend does it show, and what are its limits?
answer: METR measures not the share of solved tasks but how long a task an agent can do, in human time. It uses about 170 tasks (software engineering, machine learning, security) that professionals also did; a task’s human time is the typical time of the professionals who solved it, from seconds to many hours. A model is run on all tasks, a curve of success probability against human task time is fitted, and the 50 % time horizon is where the curve crosses 50 % (e.g. about an hour for a strong early-2025 model). It is the people’s time – not how long the model worked, or how long it can work alone. Trend: the horizon grows exponentially (a straight line on a logarithmic axis), doubling at a roughly fixed pace \(T_d\) of about 7 months, faster for models since 2023: \[H(t) \approx H_0 \cdot 2^{t / T_d}\] From seconds for GPT-2 (2019) it reached hours for 2025 models. Limits: the tasks stand alone and have an automatic check, unlike most real work; the human times are of people new to the code (maintainers can be several times faster); “solved” comes from a program, and with maintainer verdicts instead of tests the horizon shrank drastically (in one measurement from about 50 to about 8 minutes); at 80 % success the horizon is several times shorter; each estimate has a wide range (e.g. 5.3 h with a 95 % range of 2.8–12 h); and METR itself calls measurements above 16 hours unreliable with its current tasks.
keyPoints: Tasks timed by human professionals; horizon = task length at 50 % success
Human time, not the model’s working time
Exponential growth \(H(t) \approx H_0 \cdot 2^{t/T_d}\), doubling about every 7 months
Limits: standalone auto-checked tasks, newcomer human times, test-based verdicts
Higher required reliability (80 %) means a much shorter horizon; estimates have wide ranges
source: Lecture 4, slides 43–46 (the formula restates the doubling trend)

name: You are shown a benchmark number for a model. For each box of the testing process (input, model + harness, output, reference, grader, score) give one way it can fail, then state what to do before trusting the number.
answer:
The process: an input goes to the model in its harness, which produces an output; a grader (a program or a person) compares it with the reference and gives a verdict; the score is the average of the verdicts.
Input: the model may have seen the items – e.g. it recites hidden wrong options of MMLU questions. Model + harness: the same model scores several points apart in another harness or with another prompt format. Output: it is sampled, so two runs of the same model give different scores. Reference: the answer key or the tests are wrong, too strict or too weak. Grader: “the tests pass” is not “correct” – maintainers would merge only part of the test-passing patches. Score: it has a range (on 500 tasks about \(\pm 3.8\) points), depends on how attempts are counted, and hides the cost. On top of all this, Goodhart’s law: once a score is advertised, people work on the score itself.
What to do: (1) read the note under the number – which tasks, which harness, how many attempts and runs, what cost, who ran it; (2) open the tasks and check the source – a few tasks show what the benchmark really asks for, and a blog post is a hint until somebody has checked it; (3) compare with the range – a one- or two-point lead on 500 tasks is a tie; (4) measure on your own work – ten or twenty tasks from your repository, in your harness, checked by your tests and your review; this shows only large differences, but on your tasks. Do not overcorrect: changes as large as from about 2 % to over 75 % on SWE-bench are not noise. Trust a number as far as you can trace it to its tasks, harness and grader.
keyPoints: Input: contamination
Model + harness and output: setup changes and sampling move the score
Reference and grader: wrong or weak keys; passing tests ≠ correct
Score: range, attempt counting and cost; Goodhart on top
Read the note, open the tasks, compare with the range
Measure on your own tasks; very large trends are real
